rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem type is a compressed, read-only Linux filesystem embedded in small systems. A cramfs image can be used without first decompressing it.
rules.impact: Removing support for unnecessary file system types reduces the local system attack surface.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs file system is a free implementation of the Veritas file system and is not used on typical Debian servers.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the risk of exploiting drivers and untrusted kernel code.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: HFS is a legacy Apple file system. It is rarely needed on Linux servers and may contain unused code.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the potential attack surface in legacy modules.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: HFS+ (hfsplus) is used on macOS but is rarely used on Debian servers. Unnecessary modules should be disabled.
rules.impact: Disabling reduces the risk of loading unnecessary drivers and attacks via their vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: JFFS2 is intended for flash memory on embedded devices, is not used on servers, and represents unnecessary code in the kernel.
rules.impact: The presence of the unused JFFS2 kernel module increases the attack surface and creates a risk of exploiting vulnerabilities in its code.

rules.title: The overlayfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: OverlayFS is used to overlay filesystems (container scenarios). If it is not required, it is better to disable it to reduce the attack surface.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces risk, especially if the system does not use containers that depend on overlayfs.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: SquashFS is a compressed read-only file system, often used in live distributions.
rules.impact: Disabling this prevents use of malicious or uncontrolled live images.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: UDF is used for optical discs (CD/DVD/BD). It is rarely needed on server systems and can be disabled.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the kernel code base and driver vulnerability risk.

rules.title: The usb-storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The usb-storage module allows connecting USB storage devices.
rules.impact: Disabling this reduces the risk of data leakage and malware spread from external media.

rules.title: /tmp is mounted as a separate partition is configured
rules.explanation: /tmp is used for temporary files that may contain executables and scripts.
rules.impact: A separate partition for /tmp reduces the risk of execution and privileged access via temporary files.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /tmp in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev option prohibits device files on the /tmp partition, preventing users from creating special device files.
rules.impact: If nodev is missing, an attacker may create special device files and gain uncontrolled access to resources.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /tmp in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid option blocks execution of setuid/setgid bits on /tmp, which hinders privilege escalation via temporary files.
rules.impact: Without nosuid, setuid binaries placed in /tmp may be executed, enabling privileged elevation.

rules.title: Noexec is set for /tmp in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec option prohibits execution of binaries from the /tmp partition, reducing the risk of running malware uploaded to the temporary partition.
rules.impact: If noexec is missing, executables can be run on /tmp, which increases the risk of compromise.

rules.title: /dev/shm is mounted as a separate partition is configured
rules.explanation: /dev/shm is tmpfs for shared memory.
rules.impact: A separate partition allows applying noexec, nodev, and nosuid, preventing exploitation via shared memory.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /dev/shm in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev on /dev/shm prevents creation of special devices in shared memory, which reduces the attack vector.
rules.impact: The absence of nodev may allow attackers to create devices and bypass security restrictions.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /dev/shm in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid prevents use of setuid/setgid on /dev/shm and reduces the risk of privilege elevation via shared memory.
rules.impact: If nosuid is missing, attacks using setuid binaries in shared memory are possible.

rules.title: Noexec is set for /dev/shm in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Noexec prohibits executing files from /dev/shm.
rules.impact: Without this option, an attacker can run malicious programs from /dev/shm.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /home in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev prohibits creation of special devices in /home, which protects the system from user-created special files.
rules.impact: Without nodev, users may create special device files and escalate privileges.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /home in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid prevents execution of setuid/setgid programs from /home, reducing the risk of local privilege escalation.
rules.impact: If nosuid is absent, user-owned setuid binaries may be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /var in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev on /var prevents special device files from being created by processes writing to /var.
rules.impact: This reduces the risk of exploitation via special files in /var.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /var in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid on /var prevents execution of setuid/setgid programs placed under /var (for example, log/ftp directories).
rules.impact: If nosuid is missing, exploits via setuid binaries placed in /var are possible.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /var/tmp in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev prevents users and processes from creating special files in /var/tmp.
rules.impact: This reduces the likelihood of device abuse in the temporary files directory.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /var/tmp in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid prevents execution of setuid/setgid from /var/tmp, which is critical for preventing local privilege escalation.
rules.impact: If absent, users may download and execute setuid files.

rules.title: Noexec is set for /var/tmp in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Noexec on /var/tmp prevents execution of binaries and scripts from that directory.
rules.impact: Absence of noexec increases the likelihood of executing malicious binaries from temporary locations.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /var/log in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev prohibits creation of special devices in the log directory, which prevents possible security bypasses.
rules.impact: Absence of nodev provides an additional attack vector via special files.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /var/log in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid protects logs from hosting setuid programs, which could potentially lead to privilege escalation.
rules.impact: This reduces the likelihood that logs will be used as storage for setuid binaries.

rules.title: Noexec is set for /var/log in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Noexec reduces the risk of running scripts/binaries directly from /var/log.
rules.impact: Absence of this control may allow execution of code placed in logs by an attacker.

rules.title: Nodev is set for /var/log/audit in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nodev prevents creation of special devices in the audit log directory, protecting their integrity.
rules.impact: This reduces the risk of compromising audit files via special devices.

rules.title: Nosuid is set for /var/log/audit in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Nosuid protects audit logs from hosting setuid programs, which could distort audit data.
rules.impact: Maintaining log integrity is critical for forensics and monitoring.

rules.title: Noexec is set for /var/log/audit in /etc/fstab is configured
rules.explanation: Noexec prevents execution of code from the audit log directory, preserving log integrity.
rules.impact: This reduces the likelihood that logs will be used to execute malicious code.

rules.title: Repository GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: GPG keys ensure the integrity and authenticity of packages supplied from repositories.
rules.impact: Missing GPG keys increase the risk of installing forged or substituted packages.

rules.title: /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ are configured correctly
rules.explanation: Incorrect repository configuration can result in unavailable updates or use of untrusted sources.
rules.impact: Using untrusted repositories creates a risk of installing malware.

rules.title: The system is updated and security packages are installed is configured
rules.explanation: Regular updates remediate known vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: Unpatched CVEs increase the likelihood of system exploitation by attackers.

rules.title: The apparmor package is installed is configured
rules.explanation: AppArmor provides Mandatory Access Control (MAC) and restricts process actions according to profiles.
rules.impact: Absence of AppArmor deprives the system of an additional process confinement layer and increases the risk of compromise.

rules.title: The bootloader configuration (grub) includes apparmor=1 and apparmor=on is configured
rules.explanation: AppArmor must be enabled at kernel boot (bootloader parameters) so that profiles are applied from startup.
rules.impact: If AppArmor is not enabled in the bootloader, profiles may not load before services initialize.

rules.title: A password is set for the bootloader (GRUB) is configured
rules.explanation: A bootloader password prevents unauthorized changes to boot parameters and modification of the kernel/bootloader parameters with physical/local access.
rules.impact: The absence of a bootloader password allows an attacker to change kernel parameters (for example, disable AppArmor/SELinux) and bypass protections.

rules.title: Permissions and ownership of bootloader configuration files are restricted is configured
rules.explanation: Access to bootloader configuration files must be restricted (root-only) to prevent unauthorized modification.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow a local user to change boot parameters and potentially bypass security mechanisms.

rules.title: ASLR is enabled (kernel.randomize_va_space = 2)
rules.explanation: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) makes it harder to predict stack/library locations, which complicates exploitation of buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: Disabled ASLR significantly simplifies successful exploitation of vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is set to 1 or less is configured
rules.explanation: Restricting ptrace (ptrace_scope) prevents unsafe access between processes of different users.
rules.impact: Disabled or unrestricted ptrace may allow local users to interfere with other users' processes (a key privileged access risk).

rules.title: Core dumps are either disabled or that their permissions and storage location are secure (ulimit -c 0 or /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern) is configured
rules.explanation: Core dumps may contain sensitive data (passwords, keys). Restricting core file generation and permissions prevents disclosure of confidential information.
rules.impact: Unlimited core dumps increase the risk of secret data leakage when processes crash.

rules.title: /etc/motd contains an appropriate warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd (message of the day) file informs users of the acceptable use policy and warns of legal restrictions.
rules.impact: Absence of warning banners may weaken the legal position in incidents and reduce user awareness.

rules.title: The local banner is configured in /etc/issue
rules.explanation: A local banner (for example /etc/issue) provides a warning to users when logging in via the console.
rules.impact: The absence of a banner does not create a technical vulnerability, but it reduces user awareness and legal protection.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net contains a correct banner is configured
rules.explanation: The remote access banner (for example, /etc/issue.net) informs remote users of the rules and warns against unauthorized access.
rules.impact: As with the local banner, its absence reduces legal protection and user awareness.

rules.title: /etc/motd is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file must be owned by root and be read-only to prevent unauthorized banner modification.
rules.impact: A modified banner may mislead users or conceal important messages.

rules.title: /etc/issue is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file must be protected from modification by ordinary users so that banners remain trustworthy.
rules.impact: Altering the banner reduces trust and may conceal security warnings.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: Protecting /etc/issue.net ensures that remote banners are not modified by unauthorized persons.
rules.impact: An untrusted banner may mislead remote users and serve as a social engineering vector.

rules.title: The gdm3 package is not installed if a graphical interface is not required is configured
rules.explanation: If a graphical subsystem is not required on the server, it is recommended that GDM (GNOME Display Manager) be removed to reduce the attack surface.
rules.impact: Installing GDM on a server increases the number of services and potential vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The GDM configuration contains a correct banner (custom.conf or the corresponding profile) is configured
rules.explanation: GDM can display a banner at graphical session logon — it should be configured to match warning-banner policy.
rules.impact: The absence of a banner reduces user awareness and legal protection for graphical sessions.

rules.title: Disable-user-list=true is set in /etc/gdm3/greeter.dconf-defaults (or custom.conf) is configured
rules.explanation: The disable-user-list option prevents the user list from being displayed on the login screen, making it harder for an external observer to collect usernames.
rules.impact: A public user list facilitates login guessing and presents a social engineering risk.

rules.title: Automatic screen lock on idle is enabled in the GDM/GNOME configuration
rules.explanation: Automatic screen lock protects sessions from unauthorized access when the user is absent.
rules.impact: Lack of lockout increases the risk of access to open sessions.

rules.title: Lockout policies are applied globally and cannot be changed by users is configured
rules.explanation: Screen lock settings must not be user-overridable to prevent the security policy from being reset.
rules.impact: If users can disable the lock, protections against physical/local access become less effective.

rules.title: Automount policies in GDM/GNOME are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Automounting removable media in a graphical environment increases the risk of malware spread and data leakage.
rules.impact: Automounting may result in automatic execution of or access to malicious files.

rules.title: Automount policy settings are applied at the system level is configured
rules.explanation: Global policies that prohibit automounting must be reliably applied and must not be overridden by users.
rules.impact: If policies can be bypassed, the risk of malware spread remains.

rules.title: Autorun-never is enabled in GDM/environment settings
rules.explanation: The autorun-never option prevents automatic execution of multimedia/scripts when external media are connected.
rules.impact: Autorun increases the risk of automatically launching malicious code.

rules.title: System autorun-never policies cannot be overridden by users is configured
rules.explanation: As with the previous recommendation, it is important that the autorun prohibition cannot be overridden by the user.
rules.impact: If policies can be reset, the autorun risk remains.

rules.title: XDMCP is disabled in the GDM configuration
rules.explanation: XDMCP is a legacy remote X-login protocol.
rules.impact: Enabled XDMCP increases the network attack surface and may lead to unauthorized access to sessions.

rules.title: Chargen services are disabled (xinetd.d/chargen* or systemd-unit chargen*) is configured
rules.explanation: Chargen services (over TCP/UDP) are intended for testing but may be used for DoS attacks if enabled.
rules.impact: Enabled chargen services allow reflected DoS attacks.

rules.title: Daytime TCP/UDP services are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: The daytime service (ports 13/TCP and 13/UDP) returns the current system time in text form. This protocol is obsolete, does not require authentication, and must not be available on servers.
rules.impact: Legacy network services increase the attack surface.

rules.title: Discard is disabled
rules.explanation: The discard service (port 9/TCP and UDP) silently discards all received data without returning a response. This service is obsolete and is not needed on modern servers.
rules.impact: Removing unnecessary network services reduces DoS risk.

rules.title: Echo services are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: The echo service (port 7/TCP and UDP) returns every received byte to the sender. This protocol is obsolete and can be used to conduct reflected DoS attacks.
rules.impact: Disabling this prevents reflected DoS attacks.

rules.title: Legacy time services are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Legacy time TCP/UDP services (not ntpd/chrony) are not required.
rules.impact: Use of legacy time protocols introduces authentication risks.

rules.title: The tftp service (xinetd or systemd) is disabled
rules.explanation: TFTP is a simple unauthenticated protocol used for download/firmware.
rules.impact: A running TFTP service may result in unauthorized file download or leakage.

rules.title: Talk services are disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Talk is a legacy daemon for text chat between users on a system or network. The protocol does not support encryption and must not be used on modern systems.
rules.impact: Talk does not support encryption and creates a leakage risk.

rules.title: The telnet service is disabled and not installed
rules.explanation: Telnet transmits data in cleartext and must not be used.
rules.impact: Using Telnet allows credentials to be intercepted.

rules.title: Rsh (rlogin, rexec) is disabled
rules.explanation: RSH/Rlogin are legacy remote access services without encryption.
rules.impact: Use of r-services provides full unencrypted remote access.

rules.title: The rsync daemon is disabled if not in use
rules.explanation: Rsync in daemon mode opens a network port and may allow data copying without encryption.
rules.impact: An open rsync port is a common cause of data leaks.

rules.title: Ypserv is disabled
rules.explanation: NIS is a legacy centralized authentication system.
rules.impact: NIS is vulnerable to password interception and network attacks.

rules.title: Ypbind is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The NIS client (ypbind) is also obsolete and should be removed unless compatibility is required.
rules.impact: NIS does not encrypt traffic and increases the risk of credential leakage.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The RSH client must be removed to prevent use of obsolete unencrypted protocols.
rules.impact: Using the rsh client may lead to password leakage and SSH policy bypass.

rules.title: The talk client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Talk client is a legacy program for network chat.
rules.impact: Legacy talk protocols do not encrypt data and are vulnerable to interception.

rules.title: Telnet is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The Telnet client may be used to access insecure server services.
rules.impact: Telnet transmits logins and passwords in cleartext.

rules.title: Ldap-utils is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: If LDAP is not used in the infrastructure, its client packages should be removed to reduce the attack surface.
rules.impact: Unused LDAP increases the number of dependencies and vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Time synchronization is configured in /etc/ntp.conf or /etc/chrony.conf
rules.explanation: Time synchronization is important for audit and logging.
rules.impact: Inconsistent time causes audit errors and log desynchronization.

rules.title: Parameters for localhost and external sources are set in ntp.conf or chrony.conf is configured is restricted
rules.explanation: NTP restrict options limit access to the time service and prevent time spoofing.
rules.impact: Without restrict, an attacker can send malicious NTP responses.

rules.title: X Window System packages (xserver-xorg*, x11-common) are not installed on the server is configured
rules.explanation: The X Window System provides a graphical interface and increases the attack surface.
rules.impact: Removing X reduces the number of vulnerable dependencies and services.

rules.title: Send_redirects = 0 in /etc/sysctl.conf is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects parameter controls whether ICMP Redirects may be sent.
rules.impact: Enabled redirect packets allow an attacker to redirect traffic.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: IP forwarding (net.ipv4.ip_forward) should be disabled on systems that are not acting as routers.
rules.impact: Enabled forwarding allows cross-network traffic and MITM attacks.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: Source-routed packets allow the sender to specify the path and bypass filters.
rules.impact: Accepting such packets enables routing and filtering bypass.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirect messages can be used to redirect traffic to an attacker.
rules.impact: Accepting redirect packets allows traffic interception.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: Even "secure" ICMP Redirect packets must not be accepted on servers that are not gateways.
rules.impact: Allowing secure-redirect enables route manipulation.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1 is configured
rules.explanation: Logging of martian packets helps detect routing anomalies.
rules.impact: Without logging of suspicious packets, an administrator will not learn about bypass attempts.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1 is configured
rules.explanation: Ignoring ICMP Echo to broadcast addresses prevents Smurf attacks.
rules.impact: Responses to broadcasts can be used for DoS.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses = 1 is configured
rules.explanation: Ignoring bogus ICMP responses reduces the likelihood of exploiting vulnerabilities in the network stack.
rules.impact: Processing bogus ICMP messages can disrupt network communication.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1 is configured
rules.explanation: Rp_filter protects against IP spoofing by verifying that a reverse path exists for the source.
rules.impact: Disabled rp_filter allows IP address spoofing.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1 is configured
rules.explanation: SYN Cookies — a protection mechanism against SYN Flood DoS.
rules.impact: Disabled SYN cookies make the system vulnerable to DoS.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: If the system is not a router, it must not accept Router Advertisement (ICMPv6).
rules.impact: Accepting RA can change IPv6 routes and cause MITM.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 is configured
rules.explanation: As with IPv4, disabling accept_redirects for IPv6 prevents route manipulation.
rules.impact: Accepting redirects can be used to bypass routes.

rules.title: The auditd service is installed and running is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd package provides logging of user actions and system events for incident investigation.
rules.impact: Without auditing, attack sources and security policy violations cannot be identified.

rules.title: Auditd is enabled via systemctl enable auditd
rules.explanation: The auditd service must start at boot so that events are recorded from system startup.
rules.impact: Lack of autostart creates a "blind window" in logging at startup.

rules.title: The audit=1 parameter is present in the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX line of /etc/default/grub is configured
rules.explanation: To avoid losing events that occur before auditd starts, enable audit=1 in the kernel parameters.
rules.impact: Without early auditing, actions before auditd starts cannot be traced.

rules.title: The audit_backlog_limit parameter is set to at least 8192 in the bootloader configuration is configured
rules.explanation: The audit_backlog_limit parameter defines the size of the audit event buffer during kernel boot, before the auditd daemon starts. An insufficient buffer size results in loss of early-boot events.
rules.impact: A low backlog value results in loss of audit data.

rules.title: Max_log_file is configured in /etc/audit/auditd.conf
rules.explanation: Configuring a maximum log size prevents disk overflow and data loss.
rules.impact: Without log limits, the /var partition may fill up.

rules.title: Max_log_file_action != delete is configured
rules.explanation: Automatic log deletion must be disabled to preserve evidence during incidents.
rules.impact: Deleting logs makes investigation impossible.

rules.title: Space_left_action is set to halt or single in /etc/audit/auditd.conf is configured
rules.explanation: If log storage is full, the system should halt safely to prevent loss of events.
rules.impact: Ignoring log overflow leads to loss of audit data and concealment of attacks.

rules.title: Correct logrotate rotation is configured for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: Log rotation prevents overflow and preserves event history.
rules.impact: Without rotation, the file system may fill up.

rules.title: The last line of audit.rules contains -e 2 is configured
rules.explanation: Immutability of audit rules prevents an attacker from modifying them while the system is running.
rules.impact: Modifiable rules allow an attacker to conceal their actions.

rules.title: The rsyslog package is installed and active on the system is configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog is the primary logging daemon on Debian, providing centralized log collection.
rules.impact: Without a system logger, logs are lost.

rules.title: Systemctl enable rsyslog is active is configured
rules.explanation: The rsyslog service must be enabled to receive and write logs.
rules.impact: A disabled rsyslog daemon results in log loss.

rules.title: ForwardToSyslog=yes is set in /etc/systemd/journald.conf is configured
rules.explanation: Systemd-journald should forward logs to rsyslog for centralized storage and rotation.
rules.impact: Without forwarding, logs may be lost when the journal is cleared.

rules.title: Compress=yes is configured
rules.explanation: Log compression reduces file system load while retaining a long history.
rules.impact: Lack of compression may lead to disk space exhaustion.

rules.title: Storage=persistent is set in /etc/systemd/journald.conf is configured
rules.explanation: The Storage=persistent setting causes systemd-journald logs to be stored on persistent disk (/var/log/journal). By default, journald may write logs only to tmpfs, causing them to be lost on reboot.
rules.impact: Without persistent storage, logs are lost after reboot.

rules.title: Logrotate is configured for all system logs in /etc/logrotate.conf and /etc/logrotate.d/
rules.explanation: Logrotate should be configured for system logs to prevent overflow and retain history.
rules.impact: Without rotation, disk overflow is possible.

rules.title: Systemctl enable cron is active is configured
rules.explanation: Cron performs periodic tasks, including auditing, updates, and backups.
rules.impact: Disabled cron disrupts automation of system tasks.

rules.title: /etc/crontab is owned by root:root and has permissions no more permissive than 0644 is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/crontab must be owned by root with permissions 0600/0644 to prevent unauthorized editing.
rules.impact: Unauthorized crontab modification allows execution of malicious jobs.

rules.title: /etc/cron.hourly is owned by root and has permissions of 0700 or 0750 is configured
rules.explanation: The cron.hourly directory must be protected from user write access.
rules.impact: Overly permissive permissions increase the risk of malicious script injection.

rules.title: /etc/cron.daily is owned by root and has permissions of 0700 or 0750 is configured
rules.explanation: The cron.daily directory is used for daily jobs and must be accessible only to root.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions may allow script injection.

rules.title: /etc/cron.weekly is owned by root and has permissions of 0700 or 0750 is configured
rules.explanation: The cron.weekly directory must have permissions for root only.
rules.impact: Weak permissions allow execution of third-party code.

rules.title: /etc/cron.monthly is owned by root and has permissions of 0700 or 0750 is configured
rules.explanation: The cron.monthly directory is used for long-term jobs.
rules.impact: Overly permissive permissions increase the risk of malicious jobs being executed.

rules.title: /etc/cron.d is owned by root and has permissions 0700 or 0750 is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/cron.d contains system package jobs and must be protected from modification.
rules.impact: Changes to cron.d can alter the behavior of system services.

rules.title: Only authorized users are listed in allow files is configured
rules.explanation: Access to cron and at must be restricted via /etc/cron.allow and /etc/at.allow.
rules.impact: Open access allows any user to run jobs.

rules.title: Password policies are set to minlen 14 and that character classes (upper, lower, digits, others) are enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/pwquality.conf file defines minimum password length and complexity.
rules.impact: Weak password requirements make passwords easy to guess.

rules.title: Deny 5 and unlock_time 900 are set in /etc/security/faillock.conf is configured
rules.explanation: The faillock mechanism locks an account after several failed logon attempts.
rules.impact: Without restrictions, password brute-force is possible.

rules.title: ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512 in /etc/login.defs is configured
rules.explanation: The modern SHA-512 algorithm is resistant to brute-force attacks and should be used in /etc/login.defs and /etc/pam.d/ configurations.
rules.impact: Legacy MD5/DES methods provide weak password protection.

rules.title: Root can log in only via console or SSH with a key is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/securetty file must contain only valid terminals for root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized root access increases the escalation risk.

rules.title: The pam_wheel module is enabled in /etc/pam.d/su to restrict use of su
rules.explanation: The su command must be allowed only for members of the wheel or sudo group.
rules.impact: Unrestricted su access increases the risk of unauthorized root logon.

rules.title: The sudo package is installed on the system is configured
rules.explanation: The sudo package must be installed to control privilege elevation and to audit administrative commands.
rules.impact: Without sudo, root access is uncontrolled.

rules.title: Defaults use_pty is set in /etc/sudoers is configured
rules.explanation: The requiretty option enables auditing of sudo commands and protects against abuse via scripts.
rules.impact: Without a pty, sudo commands are harder to trace.

rules.title: Defaults logfile is defined in /etc/sudoers is configured
rules.explanation: Logging of sudo commands enables tracking of administrative actions.
rules.impact: Without logs it is impossible to investigate administrator actions.

rules.title: NOPASSWD is not used in sudoers is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo must require the user password to prevent automatic privilege escalation.
rules.impact: NOPASSWD allows executing commands without authentication.

rules.title: Timestamp_timeout is set in /etc/sudoers to a value of no more than 15 minutes is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo must re-prompt for a password after a defined interval (typically 15 minutes).
rules.impact: A long session timeout increases the risk of an open session being abused.

rules.title: Sudo authentication uses the SHA-512 algorithm in the PAM configuration is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo authentication must use modern algorithms (for example SHA-512 in PAM).
rules.impact: Legacy MD5 methods are weakly protected.

rules.title: INACTIVE does not exceed 35 days in /etc/default/useradd and is applied to all accounts is configured
rules.explanation: Locking an account after inactivity prevents use of forgotten accounts.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts are frequently used by attackers.

rules.title: PASS_MAX_DAYS does not exceed 365 in /etc/login.defs is configured
rules.explanation: Regular password changes reduce the risk of compromise.
rules.impact: Unlimited password lifetime increases the risk of compromise.

rules.title: PASS_WARN_AGE is at least 7 days in /etc/login.defs is configured
rules.explanation: Users should be warned in advance of password expiration (? 7 days).
rules.impact: Without a warning, the user may lose access.

rules.title: PASS_MIN_DAYS is at least 1 day in /etc/login.defs is configured
rules.explanation: A minimum interval between password changes prevents bypass of password history policy.
rules.impact: Without a restriction, the old password can be reset and immediately reused.

rules.title: Remember=5 is set in /etc/pam.d/common-password is configured
rules.explanation: The PAM remember parameter prevents reuse of N previous passwords (? 5).
rules.impact: Without a restriction, a user can reuse the same password in a cycle.

rules.title: All accounts have a non-empty password field in /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: Each account must have a password hash set in /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: Passwordless accounts are a direct compromise threat.

rules.title: System accounts (UID < 1000) have their shell set to /sbin/nologin or /bin/false is configured
rules.explanation: System accounts (UID<1000) must be locked or must not be able to log on.
rules.impact: Active system accounts create vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The root account primary group has GID 0 is configured
rules.explanation: Root must have GID 0 (root group) to ensure correct permissions and auditing.
rules.impact: An incorrect root group may grant access to unauthorized users.

rules.title: The default umask is set to 027 or more restrictive in /etc/login.defs and shell profiles is configured
rules.explanation: The umask parameter defines access permissions for newly created files and directories. The value 027 means: owner — full access, group — read/execute only, others — no access.
rules.impact: More permissive rights allow other users to read files.

rules.title: The TMOUT variable is set in /etc/profile or /etc/bashrc to a value of no more than 900 seconds is configured
rules.explanation: The TMOUT variable limits session inactivity time (? 900 seconds).
rules.impact: Without a timeout, a leftover session remains active.

rules.title: Root login via tty/SSH is prohibited (for example, PermitRootLogin prohibit-password) is configured
rules.explanation: The root password must be protected, and login must be performed only via sudo or an SSH key.
rules.impact: Open root login is a primary attack target.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist in /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: Each user is assigned a unique UID for accurate auditing and separation of duties.
rules.impact: A shared UID mixes privileges and breaks auditability.

rules.title: Home directories of all users listed in /etc/passwd exist on disk is configured
rules.explanation: Each user must have a home directory for storing personal files and security settings.
rules.impact: A missing home directory causes security and configuration issues.

rules.title: Each user owns their home directory is configured
rules.explanation: The home directory must be owned by the corresponding user; otherwise, access to another user's files may be possible.
rules.impact: Owner mismatch allows unauthorized access.

rules.title: Permissions on user home directories are no more permissive than 750 is configured
rules.explanation: Home directory permissions must restrict access by other users (no more permissive than 750).
rules.impact: Excessive permissions disclose personal files.

rules.title: Netrc files are not present in user home directories is configured
rules.explanation: Netrc stores logins and passwords for remote services.
rules.impact: Presence of .netrc allows credential compromise.

rules.title: Forward files are not present in user home directories is configured
rules.explanation: Forward may redirect mail to external addresses, disclosing user information.
rules.impact: The presence of .forward may lead to leakage of internal correspondence.

rules.title: Rhosts files are not present in user home directories is configured
rules.explanation: Rhosts allows authentication bypass when using r-utilities (rlogin, rsh).
rules.impact: The presence of .rhosts allows unauthorized remote login.

rules.title: X11Forwarding no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: X11 forwarding transmits graphical sessions over SSH.
rules.impact: Enabled X11Forwarding allows attackers to use GUI tunneling.

rules.title: The MaxAuthTries parameter in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is set to 4 or less is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries limits the number of failed SSH login attempts.
rules.impact: A large value allows brute-force attacks.

rules.title: IgnoreRhosts is set to yes in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: .rhosts and .shosts files must not be used for authentication.
rules.impact: Use of rhosts bypasses passwords.

rules.title: HostbasedAuthentication is set to no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: HostbasedAuthentication relies on trusted hosts and is not secure on open networks.
rules.impact: Using host-based authentication facilitates MITM attacks.

rules.title: PermitRootLogin is set to no or prohibit-password in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: Direct root login over SSH must be prohibited to prevent attacks against the superuser.
rules.impact: Permitting root login increases the risk of compromise.

rules.title: PermitEmptyPasswords is set to no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: Empty passwords are not permitted in order to prevent unauthorized access.
rules.impact: Empty passwords are a critical vulnerability.

rules.title: PermitUserEnvironment no is configured
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment option allows users to modify SSH environment variables.
rules.impact: A user can change SSH behavior to bypass policies.

rules.title: ClientAliveInterval (no more than 300) and ClientAliveCountMax (no more than 3) are configured in /etc/ssh/sshd_config
rules.explanation: IdleTimeout terminates idle sessions, preventing abuse.
rules.impact: Sessions left open create an access risk.

rules.title: LoginGraceTime is set to no more than 60 seconds in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: LoginGraceTime defines the login wait timeout.
rules.impact: A large value leaves dangling SSH sessions.

rules.title: The UsePAM parameter is set to yes in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: Using PAM allows centralized password and login policies to be applied.
rules.impact: Without PAM, SSH ignores global restrictions.

rules.title: AllowTcpForwarding is set to no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: TCP forwarding over SSH allows bypassing filters.
rules.impact: Allowed forwarding may be used to tunnel attacks.

rules.title: MaxStartups is configured in /etc/ssh/sshd_config (recommended value: 10:30:60)
rules.explanation: The MaxStartups parameter limits concurrent unauthenticated SSH login attempts.
rules.impact: Without a limit, a DoS is possible through many open connections.

rules.title: The MaxSessions parameter is set to 10 or less in /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: MaxSessions limits the number of concurrent SSH sessions for a single connection.
rules.impact: Without a limit, resource exhaustion is possible.

rules.title: The aide package is installed on the system is configured
rules.explanation: AIDE is used to monitor file system integrity and detect changes.
rules.impact: Absence of AIDE precludes change control capability.

rules.title: Permissions are 644 and the owner is root:root is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd must be readable by all, but writable only by root.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow modification of system credentials.

rules.title: /etc/shadow permissions are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow stores passwords and must be accessible only to root and the shadow group.
rules.impact: Access to shadow discloses password hashes.

rules.title: /etc/group is owned by root:root and has permissions 644 is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/group defines user group membership.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow users to change group membership.

rules.title: /etc/gshadow permissions are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow stores protected group data.
rules.impact: Access to gshadow discloses administrative group membership.

rules.title: No /etc/shadow entries have an empty password field is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow must not contain empty password fields.
rules.impact: An empty password field allows logon without authentication.

rules.title: /etc/passwd contains no lines starting with the '+' character is configured
rules.explanation: "+" entries in /etc/passwd indicate legacy NIS integration and must be removed.
rules.impact: Presence of "+" may enable unknown external accounts.

rules.title: /etc/shadow contains no lines starting with the '+' character is configured
rules.explanation: Stale NIS entries in /etc/shadow increase the risk of authentication bypass.
rules.impact: "+" entries can override local passwords.

rules.title: /etc/group contains no lines starting with the '+' character is configured
rules.explanation: "+" in /etc/group indicates a legacy NIS binding.
rules.impact: May result in unintended group membership.

rules.title: Only the root account has UID 0 in /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: Only root should have UID 0.
rules.impact: Multiple UID 0 accounts are a critical security error.

rules.title: All GIDs specified in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: Every group specified in /etc/passwd must exist in /etc/group.
rules.impact: A nonexistent group causes access control problems.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist in /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: UID must be unique for each user.
rules.impact: Duplicate UIDs allow users to act on behalf of others.

rules.title: There are no duplicate GID values in /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: Each group must have a unique GID.
rules.impact: Duplicate GIDs cause incorrect privilege inheritance.

rules.title: /etc/passwd contains no duplicate usernames is configured
rules.explanation: User names must be unique to uniquely identify accounts.
rules.impact: Duplicate names can conceal attacker activity.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist in /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: Group names must be unique to avoid confusion in access rights and group policy control.
rules.impact: Duplicate group names make security management more difficult.
